newsitem.title: FRANCE: Cr Lyonnais plan to be submitted to Brussels this week.
newsitem.headline: Cr Lyonnais plan to be submitted to Brussels this week.

text.p: France said on Tuesday it would submit a plan to privatise struggling state-owned bank Credit Lyonnais to the European Commission later this week for approval but its cost would not be known until it was implemented.
The government, however, could face a stiff fight to win approval from the Commission and from the bank's rivals for the rescue.
Some newspapers have said the government may have to pour 30 billion francs ($5.2 billion) into the bank to ready it for sale. But a finance ministry official called such figures "pure speculation."
"We won't know (the full cost) until we've started to put the plan into operation," the official said.
The cost of the rescue is expected to partly reflect the size of capital losses from asset disposals demanded by the Commission in exchange for approving new state aid.
Finance Minister Jean Arthuis promised to submit the plan, already weeks overdue, at a meeting on Monday with European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert in Brussels.
Once the country's flagship bank, Credit Lyonnais has already received billions of francs in state money after a lending spree that backfired and led to huge losses.
The Commission could take four months to consider the bail-out which the government has vowed will be the last. "We may be looking at June to hear from the Commission," said a source.
The Commission has already said it is concerned about the public money poured into the bank and French bank Societe Generale announced on Monday plans for a legal challenge.

The fresh state aid would be on top of 45 billion francs the bank got from the taxpayer in 1995 and 3.9 billion in emergency help it received last year to allow it to post a modest 1996 first half profit of 67 million francs.

Newspapers have said 15 to 20 billion francs in new money would be needed to scrap heavy financial penalties imposed on the bank under the 1995 rescue. The rest would be needed to recapitalise it and boost solvability ratios to attract a buyer.
The Commission has been pushing Credit Lyonnais to step up asset sales to comply with conditions it slapped on the bank in exchange for approval of the 1995 rescue.
And Societe Generale has said it should not get to keep its profitable operations that include its lucrative U.S. and Asian investment bank activities while being bailed out by taxpayers.

Credit Lyonnais is expected to have to unwind much of its retail banking network in western Europe outside France as part of the restructuring plan to ready it for sale but it will put up a stiff fight to keep its merchant bank activities.
"It would be a universal bank in France with retail and investment activities but just keep its investment bank activities outside France," said someone close to the dossier.
The bank said on Tuesday it would sell its Swedish retail banking arm Credit Lyonnais Bank Sverige AB to Trygg Banken AB of Sweden. It said the impact on its finances would be neutral.
Credit Lyonnais chairman Jean Peyrelevade has warned disposal of the European retail network could mean up to nine billion francs ($1.6 billion) in capital losses.
Many of the bank's assets were bought at peak prices and their sale would trigger capital losses that would have an impact on its solvability ratios and its recapitalisation needs.

Peyrelevade said the bank may need a tier one ratio -- an international solvency ratio -- of six percent, up from a current 4.5 percent, to be privatised. Each percentage point increase in its tier one ratio would cost eight billion francs.
The centre-right government hopes to privatise the bank quickly but industry sources say a sale is unlikely until 1998. ($ = 5.748 French Francs)
